title: What I Do When a Parent, Guardian, or Student Emails Me Re: Make-Up Work or "How to Get My Grade Up" ake-up-work-or-how-to-get-my-grade-up
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a teacher's question at a California PD session about time-consuming "how do I get my grade up" emails from students and parents, Stuart explains why he replaced email replies with in-person meetings. He diagnoses two problems with emailed responses: email is easy to ignore, and responding well requires far more teacher effort (10+ minutes of gradebook analysis) than the student invested in asking (a 30-second message), an imbalance that predicts low follow-through. His alternative is a standing offer of a 15-minute meeting (after school, during lunch, or before school) where he sits with the student, reviews the gradebook together, and hands them an index card listing the three most promising ways to improve their grade, sometimes using the remaining time to get the student started on the work itself. Stuart frames this as satisficing, an example of a repetitive workload inefficiency that a small structural change can resolve, benefiting both the teacher's time and the student's actual follow-through.
points: Stuart identifies two structural reasons emailed grade-improvement advice fails: email is easy to ignore, and the reply demands far more teacher effort than the student's original message invested.
His replacement is a standing offer of a 15-minute in-person meeting rather than a written reply, shifting the format from something ignorable to something the student has to show up for.

In the meeting, he analyzes the gradebook together with the student in real time and hands them a physical index card listing the three most promising action items, making the plan concrete and portable.

He frames the whole practice as an example of "satisficing" — finding a good-enough, sustainable response to a repetitive workload problem rather than over-investing in a solution that doesn't actually change outcomes.
quotes: Email is supremely ignorable. Lots of us ignore lots of emails just because as finite creatures we have to. There's too much coming at us. Sometimes, it just comes down to ignore emails or ignore sleep.

You're trading a 30-second "What can I do to improve my grade?" email for 10+ minutes of gradebook analysis, summarization, and advising. It's not that it's an unfair trade — it's just that it's an imbalanced one.
Instead, I like to offer a 15-minute meeting, with the following slots in order of my preference: After school, during lunch, before school.

As we find action items, I grab an index card and write them down for the student. Once we find the three most promising avenues for improving their grade, I hand them the index card and ask them if they'd like to use the rest of their time with me getting started on the work.
I've spent less effort analyzing their gradebook than I would have responding to the email, and they've gained a lot more than they would have had I emailed back a summary with advice.
